one_sentence_story: In 1968, Robert Zajonc proved the Mere Exposure Effect — simply encountering neutral nonsense words, unfamiliar symbols, or strangers' faces 5 to 25 times makes us rate them warmer and more likable (even after 1-ms subliminal flashes!) because faster visual processing feels safe and pleasant.
so_what_for_you: Give healthy new foods, complex music, and unfamiliar colleagues **5 to 10 spaced encounters** before judging them — and never confuse 'I've seen this claim/brand 25 times on my feed' with 'this is actually trustworthy'.

jargon_map.plain: growing warmer toward a person, word, face, or melody simply because you have encountered it repeatedly without harm
jargon_map.analogy: a footpath through snow feeling smoother on trip #10 than trip #1

jargon_map.plain: the brain processing a repeated image or sound faster and with less effort in sensory cortex, then experiencing that ease as positive liking
jargon_map.analogy: mistaking 'easy on the eyes' for 'good in the world'

jargon_map.plain: finding that subliminal 1-ms flashes raise liking even when conscious recognition sits at 50% pure chance
jargon_map.analogy: warming up to a face before remembering the name

jargon_map.plain: preferring your mirror-reversed face because you see it daily while friends prefer your true camera orientation
jargon_map.analogy: two audiences trained on opposite flips of the same face

jargon_map.plain: eventual boredom dip when simple stimuli are hammered dozens of times back-to-back without rest spacing
jargon_map.analogy: loving a song on play #10 and muting it on play #100
